record.original_question: Let f be a nonzero integrable function on R such that the set {x in R : f(x) != 0} has finite Lebesgue measure. Suppose f tiles R at some level w with a translation set Lambda subset R of bounded density. Must Lambda have a periodic structure, meaning that Lambda can be represented as a disjoint union of finitely many arithmetic progressions of the form a_j Z + b_j with a_j > 0?

evidence.quote: Let f be a nonzero function in L1(R), and suppose that the set {x : f(x) != 0} has finite measure. If f tiles at some level w by a translation set Lambda subset R of bounded density, does it follows that Lambda has a periodic structure?

We say that a set Lambda subset R has a periodic structure if it can be represented as a disjoint union of finitely many arithmetic progressions, namely Lambda = union from j=1 to N of (a_j Z + b_j), where a_j, b_j are real numbers and a_j > 0.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ be a nonzero function such that the set $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) \neq 0\}$ has finite Lebesgue measure. A discrete set $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$ is said to have bounded density if $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \#(\Lambda \cap [x, x+1]) < \infty$. We say that $f$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ at level $w \in \mathbb{C}$ by the translation set $\Lambda$ if
$$\sum_{\lambda \in \Lambda} f(x - \lambda) = w \quad \text{for almost every } x \in \mathbb{R},$$
with the series converging absolutely a.e. We say that $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$ has a periodic structure if it can be written as a disjoint union of finitely many arithmetic progressions
$$\Lambda = \bigsqcup_{j=1}^{N} (a_j \mathbb{Z} + b_j),$$
where $a_j > 0$ and $b_j \in \mathbb{R}$.

Question: Suppose $f$ tiles $\mathbb{R}$ at some level $w$ by a translation set $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}$ of bounded density. Must $\Lambda$ necessarily have a periodic structure?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears as an explicitly stated open question in the Kolountzakis–Lev survey on tiling by translates of a function (2020), and subsequent literature (e.g., later work by Kolountzakis and collaborators on tiling, spectrality and aperiodicity, 2023) continues to treat it as open. No published resolution was found.
